terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with the accusative
evidence: Cic. Q. Fr. 1.3.5: cum amīcī partim dēseruerint mē, partim etiam prōdiderint (Lewis & Short)
Verg. A. 10.600: frātrem nē dēsere frāter (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Leave someone or something one should stand by: friends, an army, a post, a cause. Narrower than relinquere and, from its military use, often implying cowardice (Lewis & Short). Of things, “fail, give out”.

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with the accusative
evidence: Ter. Phorm. 1.2.22: mē fīliīs relinquont quasi magistrum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The general word for leaving a person or a place behind, which need not blame (Lewis & Short); also “leave over, bequeath”.

terms.gloss: leave in the lurch, let down
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with the accusative
evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 117: indūxit, dēcēpit, dēstituit, adversāriīs trādidit (Lewis & Short)
Phaedr. 5.10: nōn tē dēstituit animus, sed vīrēs meae
terms.comment: Leave someone alone when he relies on you. Its first sense is “set down, place” (Livy, Plautus) (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: cum amīcī partim dēseruerint mē, partim etiam prōdiderint
phrases.english: since some of my friends have abandoned me and some have even betrayed me

phrases.latin: nōtāsque palūdēs dēserit atque altam suprā volat ardea nūbem
phrases.english: and the heron leaves its familiar marshes and flies above the high clouds

phrases.latin: nōn tē dēstituit animus, sed vīrēs meae
phrases.english: it was not my courage that let you down, but my strength
